questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish conditional from absolute convergence at an endpoint.
questions.stem: Revision sheet 7 of the group asks why the series sum of x^n over n converges at x = -1 but not at x = 1. Explain the difference in kind at the two endpoints.

answer.exemplar: At x = 1 the series becomes the harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ..., whose terms are positive and whose partial sums grow without bound, so it diverges. At x = -1 the series becomes the alternating harmonic series -1 + 1/2 - 1/3 + ..., whose terms alternate in sign and decrease in magnitude to zero, so the alternating series test gives convergence. The convergence at -1 is only conditional, because the absolute values give back the divergent harmonic series, so the two endpoints fail in quite different ways.

questions.explanation: At x = 1 the series is the harmonic series and diverges; at x = -1 it is the alternating harmonic series and converges. That convergence is conditional, since absolute values give the harmonic series.
questions.hint: Write out the two endpoint series explicitly.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain the repeating coefficient pattern of a second-order quotient.
questions.stem: A third revision card notes that 1/(1 + x + x^2) has the pattern 1, -1, 0, 1, -1, 0 in its coefficients. Explain where that pattern comes from.

answer.exemplar: The denominator 1 + x + x^2 multiplies the geometric series in 1 minus x, because (1 + x + x^2)(1 - x) = 1 - x^3. Since 1 over (1 - x) is 1 + x + x^2 + x^3 and so on, the quotient 1 over (1 + x + x^2) equals (1 - x) over (1 - x^3), and the second factor expands as 1 + x^3 + x^6 and so on. Multiplying by 1 - x then gives coefficients 1, -1, 0 repeating with period three, exactly the pattern observed.

questions.explanation: Since (1 + x + x^2)(1 - x) = 1 - x^3, the quotient is (1 - x) over (1 - x^3), and expanding 1 over (1 - x^3) as 1 + x^3 + x^6 gives the repeating pattern 1, -1, 0 with period three.
questions.hint: Multiply the denominator by 1 - x and look at what you get.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Derive the interval of convergence of a series with harmonic-type terms.
questions.stem: Revision sheet 31 of the group derives why the series sum of x^n over n has a conditionally convergent endpoint and a divergent one. Explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: The series sum of x^n over n has radius 1, so it converges for |x| below 1 and the two endpoints must be examined separately. At x = 1 the series is 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ..., the harmonic series, whose partial sums grow without bound, so it diverges. At x = -1 the series is the alternating harmonic series, whose terms decrease in magnitude to zero, so the alternating series test gives convergence. The convergence there is conditional, because taking absolute values reproduces the divergent harmonic series.

questions.explanation: The radius is 1, so the endpoints need separate tests: at x = 1 the series is the divergent harmonic series, and at x = -1 it is the alternating harmonic series, which converges conditionally.
questions.hint: Test each endpoint with the relevant series.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Radius unaffected by finitely many coefficients
questions.learningObjective: Explain why deleting finitely many terms preserves the radius.
questions.stem: Revision sheet 37 of the group asks why removing the first five terms of a power series does not change its radius of convergence. Explain the argument.

answer.exemplar: A power series converges absolutely for every x strictly inside its radius and diverges for every x outside it, and this behaviour is governed by the tail of the series, since finitely many terms cannot affect convergence. The tail of the series beginning at the sixth term has the same ratio of successive terms as the original series, so the ratio test gives exactly the same radius. Removing finitely many terms therefore shifts the first few coefficients of the power series but leaves the interval of convergence and the radius untouched.

questions.explanation: Finitely many terms cannot affect convergence, and the tail has the same ratio of successive terms as the whole series, so the radius is unchanged. Only the first few coefficients of the power series change.
questions.hint: Convergence depends on the tail of the series, not its first terms.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain the meaning of conditional convergence at an endpoint.
questions.stem: Card thirteen in the pack asks the group to explain why the series sum of x^n over n is called conditionally convergent at x = -1. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: At x = -1 the series sum of (-1)^n over n is the alternating harmonic series, and its terms alternate in sign while decreasing in magnitude to zero, so the alternating series test guarantees convergence. It is only conditional, because the sum of the absolute values is the harmonic series, which diverges. A series converges absolutely when its absolute values form a convergent series, and here they do not, so the convergence at that single endpoint is a cancellation effect rather than a genuine summability of the positive terms.

questions.explanation: At x = -1 the series is the alternating harmonic series and converges by the alternating test, but its absolute values form the divergent harmonic series. Such cancellation-based convergence is called conditional.
questions.hint: Compare the series with the series of its absolute values.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how growing coefficients coexist with a convergent series.
questions.stem: The Tuesday group session clarifies why the series 1/(1 - x - x^2) has coefficients that grow without bound even though the series itself converges for |x| below 1 over the golden ratio. Explain.

answer.exemplar: Multiplying the series by 1 - x - x^2 and comparing coefficients gives a_n = a_{n-1} + a_{n-2} with a_0 = a_1 = 1, so the coefficients follow the Fibonacci rule and grow like a constant times the golden ratio to the n. The radius of convergence is the reciprocal of that growth rate, because a power series converges precisely when the terms a_n x^n tend to zero, and a_n x^n behaves like the constant times the golden ratio times x to the n. The coefficients therefore grow even though the series converges for every x inside the radius.

questions.explanation: The coefficients follow a_n = a_{n-1} + a_{n-2}, so they grow like the golden ratio to the n, and the radius is the reciprocal of that rate. The series converges because a_n x^n tends to zero inside the radius.
questions.hint: Convergence depends on the terms a_n x^n, not on the coefficients alone.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Compute a radius for a series with both a scale factor and a polynomial divisor.
questions.stem: Revision sheet 58 of the group computes the radius of convergence of the series sum of 10 to the n times x to the n over n.
questions.explanation: The ratio of successive terms is 10x times n over (n+1), which tends to 10x, so the series converges for |10x| below 1 and the radius is 0.1. The factor 1 over n does not alter the limiting ratio, only the speed of convergence.
questions.hint: The radius is 1 divided by the limiting ratio.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Radius when the ratio test stalls
questions.learningObjective: Compute the limit of a ratio of factorial coefficients.
questions.stem: Card seventeen in the pack lists the coefficients 1, 1, 1/2, 1/6, 1/24 and asks for the limit of the ratio of successive coefficients.
questions.explanation: The ratio of successive coefficients is n over (n+1), which tends to 0, and that is why the radius of convergence is infinite. The coefficients shrink faster than any geometric rate, so the ratio test succeeds for every x.
questions.hint: Divide each coefficient by the one before it and take the limit.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Find a ratio limit and radius for a series with a doubled factorial.
questions.stem: The Wednesday group session asks for the limit of the ratio of successive coefficients of the series sum of x^n over the factorial of 2n, and then for the radius of convergence.

options.text: The ratio limit is 1 and the radius is 1
options.misconception: ignores the doubled factorial in the denominator

options.text: The ratio limit is x and the radius is 1
options.misconception: treats the ratio as if the factorial were absent

options.text: The ratio limit is 0 and the radius is 1
options.misconception: pairs a zero ratio limit with a radius of 1

options.text: The ratio limit is 0 and the radius is infinite

questions.explanation: The ratio of successive coefficients is x^2 over (2n+2)(2n+1), which tends to 0 for every fixed x, so the radius of convergence is infinite. A ratio limit of 0 is what the ratio test needs to succeed everywhere.
questions.hint: Divide the nth coefficient by the one before it.
